'''Edward I. Solomon''' (born 1946) is the [[Monroe Spaght|Monroe E. Spaght]] Professor of Chemistry at [[Stanford University]].  He is an elected member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]],<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title=National Academy of Sciences Member Directory - Edward I. Solomon|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/edward-i-solomon-pihj0q/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190324140113/http://www.nasonline.org/member-directory/members/20009981.html |archive-date=2019-03-24 }}</ref> a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]], and a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Edward I. Solomon {{!}} Department of Chemistry|url=https://chemistry.stanford.edu/people/edward-i-solomon|access-date=2021-05-17|website=chemistry.stanford.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=American Academy of Arts and Sciences - Edward Ira Solomon|url=https://www.amacad.org/person/edward-ira-solomon|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210610231136/https://www.amacad.org/person/edward-ira-solomon |archive-date=2021-06-10 }}</ref> He has been profiled in the [[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="pnasprofile">{{Cite journal | last1 = Zagorski | first1 = N. | title = Profile of Edward I. Solomon| doi = 10.1073/pnas.0606007103 | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences | volume = 103 | issue = 35 | pages = 12963–12965 | year = 2006 | pmid = 16924096 | pmc =1559735 | bibcode = 2006PNAS..10312963Z | doi-access = free }}</ref> He has been a longtime collaborator with many scientists, including his colleague at Stanford University [[Keith Hodgson]] for the study of metalloenzyme active sites by x-ray spectroscopy, along with the synthetic chemists [[Richard H. Holm]], [[Stephen J. Lippard]], [[Lawrence Que Jr.]] and [[Kenneth Karlin (chemist)|Kenneth D. Karlin]].

== Early life and education ==
Solomon grew up in [[North Miami Beach, Florida|North Miami Beach]], [[Florida]]. In his junior year of high school, he became involved in a local program that allowed exceptional students to work with university professors. Solomon conducted research with a professor at the [[University of Miami]], using biochemistry and chromatography to study [[indole]]s, which led to him becoming Florida's first-ever finalist for the [[Westinghouse Science Talent Search]] in 1964.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Zagorski|first=Nick|date=2006-08-29|title=Profile of Edward I. Solomon|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|language=en|volume=103|issue=35|pages=12963–12965|doi=10.1073/pnas.0606007103|issn=0027-8424|pmid=16924096|pmc=1559735|bibcode=2006PNAS..10312963Z|doi-access=free}}</ref>

He then studied chemistry at [[Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute|Renesselaer Polytechnic Institute]], graduating with a B.S. degree in 1968. During his undergraduate, he worked with Prof. Sam Wait and Prof. Henry Hollinger in theoretical chemistry.<ref name=":0" /> Solomon went on to [[Princeton University]] to conduct graduate studies with [[Physical chemistry|physical chemist]] Prof. Donald McClure, where he studied the [[Jahn–Teller effect]] in the excited states of [[Manganese|Mn<sup>2+</sup>]] ions in RbMnF<sub>3</sub>.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Solomon|first1=Edward I.|last2=McClure|first2=Donald S.|date=1972-09-01|title=<nowiki>Jahn-Teller Effect in the $^{4}T_{1g}(I)$ State of ${\mathrm{Mn}}^{++}$ in RbMn${\mathrm{F}}_{3}$. II</nowiki>|url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevB.6.1697|journal=Physical Review B|volume=6|issue=5|pages=1697–1708|doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.6.1697|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Solomon|first1=Edward I.|last2=McClure|first2=Donald S.|date=1974-06-01|title=<nowiki>Comparison of the Jahn-Teller effect in four triply degenerate states of ${\mathrm{Mn}}^{++}$ in RbMn${\mathrm{F}}_{3}$</nowiki>|url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevB.9.4690|journal=Physical Review B|volume=9|issue=11|pages=4690–4718|doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.9.4690|url-access=subscription}}</ref>  Shortly after Solomon received his Ph.D. in chemistry in 1972, his advisor McClure went on sabbatical and asked Solomon to stay and help oversee his research group. At this time, McClure and Prof. [[Thomas G. Spiro]] hosted a symposium that hosted many leaders in physical inorganic chemistry. It was at this symposium that Solomon decided he wanted to work with Prof. [[Harry B. Gray]] during his post-doctoral studies.

Solomon spent a year in Copenhagen, Denmark at the [[Hans Christian Ørsted Institute]] to work as a postdoctoral fellow under Prof. Carl J. Ballhausen.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Solomon|first1=Edward I.|last2=Ballhausen|first2=C. J.|date=1975-01-01|title=Identification of the structure of the 3T1g (I) ← 3A2g band in the Ni(H2O)6 ++ complex|url=https://doi.org/10.1080/00268977500100191|journal=Molecular Physics|volume=29|issue=1|pages=279–299|doi=10.1080/00268977500100191|issn=0026-8976|url-access=subscription}}</ref> He then moved to [[California Institute of Technology|Caltech]] with to do postdoctoral research with Prof. [[Harry B. Gray]] from 1974 to 1975.<ref name=":1" />

==Research==
Solomon began his independent career in late 1975 at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] as an assistant professor, where he continued to study blue copper proteins.<ref name=":0" /> In 1981, he was promoted to the rank of full professor, and in 1982 he moved to [[Stanford University]].<ref name=":1" /> At this point, bioinorganic chemistry became the dominant focus of his laboratory.

Solomon's research focuses on the spectroscopic study of metal-containing enzymes involved in electron transfers and oxygen activation, and small molecules mimicking the active sites of these enzymes. These include copper-containing enzymes such as [[azurin]], [[plastocyanin]] and [[laccase]],<ref name="Laccase">{{cite journal |last1=Allendorf |first1=M D |last2=Spira |first2=D J |last3=Solomon |first3=E I |title=Low-temperature magnetic circular dichroism studies of native laccase: spectroscopic evidence for exogenous ligand bridging at a trinuclear copper active site. |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |date=1985 |volume=82 |issue=10 |pages=3063–3067 |issn=0027-8424|pmc=397714 |pmid=2987909 |doi=10.1073/pnas.82.10.3063 |bibcode=1985PNAS...82.3063A |doi-access=free }}</ref> as well as [[Non-heme iron protein|non-heme iron enzymes]] such as [[4-hydroxymandelate synthase|(4-hydroxy)mandelate synthase]] and [[4-Hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase|(4-hydroxyphenyl)pyruvate dioxygenase]]. He is an expert in [[magnetic circular dichroism]] spectroscopy.<ref name="pnasprofile" />

=== Research highlights ===

* Elucidation of the [[tyrosinase]] dicopper active site mechanism<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wilcox|first1=Dean E.|last2=Porras|first2=Arturo G.|last3=Hwang|first3=Yeong T.|last4=Lerch|first4=Konrad|last5=Winkler|first5=Marjorie E.|last6=Solomon|first6=Edward I.|date=1985|title=Substrate analog binding to the coupled binuclear copper active site in tyrosinase|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/pdf/10.1021/ja00299a043|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=107|issue=13|pages=4015–4027|doi=10.1021/ja00299a043|bibcode=1985JAChS.107.4015W |issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription}}</ref>
* Demonstration that a trinuclear copper active site exists in the [[laccase]] enzyme<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Allendorf|first1=M. D.|last2=Spira|first2=D. J.|last3=Solomon|first3=E. I.|date=1985-05-01|title=Low-temperature magnetic circular dichroism studies of native laccase: spectroscopic evidence for exogenous ligand bridging at a trinuclear copper active site|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|language=en|volume=82|issue=10|pages=3063–3067|doi=10.1073/pnas.82.10.3063|issn=0027-8424|pmid=2987909|pmc=397714|bibcode=1985PNAS...82.3063A|doi-access=free}}</ref>
* Demonstration of the [[entatic state]] of the blue copper protein
* Development of Variable Temperature, Variable Field (VTVH) [[magnetic circular dichroism]] (MCD) spectroscopy to study [[Non-heme iron protein|non-heme iron enzyme]] active sites
* Development of metal L-edge, ligand K-edge [[x-ray absorption spectroscopy]] and [[Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering|resonant inelastic x-ray scattering]] to investigate metal-ligand covalency.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Glaser|first1=Thorsten|last2=Hedman|first2=Britt|last3=Hodgson|first3=Keith O.|last4=Solomon|first4=Edward I.|date=2000-12-01|title=Ligand K-Edge X-ray Absorption Spectroscopy: A Direct Probe of Ligand−Metal Covalency|url=https://doi.org/10.1021/ar990125c|journal=Accounts of Chemical Research|volume=33|issue=12|pages=859–868|doi=10.1021/ar990125c|pmid=11123885|issn=0001-4842|url-access=subscription}}</ref>
